title: Who came to the Stuyvesant; impressions of Gene Williams
summary: Blumberg describes the dancers, Village crowd and critics at the Stuyvesant, then Gene Williams's personality and the ridicule jazz fans face.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Another thing I'd like to know is who came to the Stuyvesant?

Well, I guess there were a lot of young couples from around New York. I mean, most of the... I was just a visitor to New York and I didn't know too much about who these people were. There were some dancers from Harlem, from uptown, and people from the village, from Greenwich Village, who were interested in jazz. But there seemed to be... Most of the people just seemed to be young couples going someplace to dance, I guess. I mean, that might not... Maybe the first week or so it was jazz enthusiasts, but after that I think there were a large... There was a large number of dancers.
Would you see musicians, critics, celebrities there too?

Well, at first there were quite a few... Critics there. I think that kind of tapered off after a little while. I ran into Buckland Moon in New York recently whom I hadn't seen since the Stuyvesant days. I'm pretty sure I used to see him there often. Uh... Did you, uh...
Do you have any impression of Gene Williams or something I wanted to ask you about?

Well, Gene was a... a very bright guy. His initial, uh... impact, I think, was that of a kind of very well-educated, very polite, and somewhat shy, I believe. At least this was the first impression. Uh... With, uh... a kind of a sense of humor. I mean, he seemed to be, as I remember him, always on the pleasant kidding side. Although, uh... He might have been too much on that. I mean, maybe, uh... Maybe he was one of these people that smiles all the time, uh... regardless of, uh... how they feel, but, uh... Uh... He seemed to be a very, very, uh... pleasant fellow. At the same time, very intense about what he was doing, about jazz.
Well, there was a lot of this guy's hostility in this kidding?

No, I don't think, uh... hostility, but I don't think he, uh... I don't think he was a person who, um... showed how he felt at any particular moment. I think he was more, uh... one of us who wears a mask, you know.

Defensive kind of thing, in other words. Yeah, yeah. Just... It's always been interesting to me, uh... the musicians and the... uh... people who follow jazz, are constantly forced to put up this kind of defensive thing, I think, if you get involved in the thing.

Yeah, well, particularly with this kind of music, uh... you're open to a lot of ridicule, and, uh... there are always the, uh... the know-nothings who, uh... who give constant mockery at every effort to, uh... help the music along. I mean, I imagine bringing Bonk to New York probably exposed him to all kinds of... remarks around New York, so... Well, there's a lot of nudniks, you know,
who caught up with these 19th century ideas of progress. I think they ought to get up to date. Yeah. You know what I mean? Yeah. And they really don't look at things
in any kind of long view

or any kind of perspective. That's right. They really, that thinking is very much out of date. That's my belief, anyway. I'll have to put some of myself in there. One thing that interested me was... your description of the first time you ever came to the Stuyvesant, and you're approaching the place. Yeah.
